entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5259"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 36</title> <div sID="gen7847" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Job.36.1-Job.36.33">Job 36:1-33</reference>.<div eID="gen7847" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7848" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5259"/>1-2. Elihu maintains that afflictions are to the godly disciplinary, in order to lead them to attain a higher moral worth, and that the reason for their continuance is not, as the friends asserted, on account of the sufferer's extraordinary guilt, but because the discipline has not yet attained its object, namely, to lend him to humble himself penitently before God (<reference osisRef="Isa.9.13">Is 9:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.5.3">Jr 5:3</reference>). This is Elihu's fourth speech. He thus exceeds the ternary number of the others. Hence his formula of politeness (<reference osisRef="Job.36.2">Job 36:2</reference>). Literally, "Wait yet but a little for me." Bear with me a little farther. I have yet (much, <reference osisRef="Job.32.18-Job.32.20">Job 32:18-20</reference>). There are Chaldeisms in this verse, agreeably to the view that the scene of the book is near the Euphrates and the Chaldees. <div eID="gen7848" type="x-p"/>

Even the "ransom" by Jesus Christ (<reference osisRef="Job.33.24">Job 33:24</reference>) will be of no avail to wilful despisers (<reference osisRef="Heb.10.26-Heb.10.29">He 10:26-29</reference>).<div eID="gen7873" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7874" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with his stroke--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Job.34.26">Job 34:26</reference>). This accords better with the verb in the parallel clause, which ought to be translated, "Let not the great ransom (of money, which thou canst give) seduce thee (Margin, turn thee aside, as if thou couldst deliver thyself from "wrath" by it). Job had wished for death (<reference osisRef="Job.3.3-Job.3.9">Job 3:3-9</reference>, &c.).<div eID="gen7876" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7877" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">night--</hi>(<reference osisRef="John.9.4">Joh 9:4</reference>).<div eID="gen7877" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7878" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">when--</hi>rather, "whereby."<div eID="gen7878" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7879" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cut off--</hi>literally, "ascend," as the corn cut and lifted upon the wagon or stack (<reference osisRef="Job.36.26">Job 36:26</reference>); so "cut off," "disappear."<div eID="gen7879" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7880" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in their place--</hi>literally, "under themselves"; so, without moving from their place, on the spot, suddenly (<reference osisRef="Job.40.12">Job 40:12</reference>) [Maurer]. Umbreit's translation: "To ascend (which is really, as thou wilt find to thy cost, to descend) to the people below" (literally, "under themselves"), answers better to the parallelism and the Hebrew. Thou pantest for death as desirable, but it is a "night" or region of darkness; thy fancied ascent (amelioration) will prove a descent (deterioration) (<reference osisRef="Job.10.22">Job 10:22</reference>); therefore desire it not. <div eID="gen7880" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5284"/><div sID="gen7895" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5284"/>27-28. The marvellous formation of rain (so <reference osisRef="Job.5.9">Job 5:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.5.10">10</reference>).<div eID="gen7895" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7896" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">maketh small--</hi>Rather, "He draweth (up) to Him, He attracts (from the earth below) the drops of water; they (the drops of water) pour down rain, (which is) His vapor." "Vapor" is in apposition with "rain," marking the way in which rain is formed; namely, from the vapor drawn up by God into the air and then condensed into drops, which fall (<reference osisRef="Ps.147.8">Psa 147:8</reference>). The suspension of such a mass of water, and its descent not in a deluge, but in drops of vapory rain, are the marvel. The selection of this particular illustration of God's greatness forms a fit prelude to the storm in which God appears (<reference osisRef="Job.40.1">Job 40:1</reference>). <div eID="gen7896" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5287"/><div sID="gen7902" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5287"/><hi type="bold">30. light--</hi>lightning.<div eID="gen7902" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7903" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">it--</hi>His tabernacle (<reference osisRef="Job.36.29">Job 36:29</reference>). The light, in an instant spread over the vast mass of dark clouds, forms a striking picture.<div eID="gen7903" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7904" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">spread--</hi>is repeated from <reference osisRef="Job.36.29">Job 36:29</reference> to form an antithesis. "He spreads not only clouds, but light."<div eID="gen7904" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7905" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">covereth the bottom--</hi>roots.<div eID="gen7905" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7906" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of the sea--</hi>namely, with the light. In the storm the depths of ocean are laid bare; and the light "covers" them, at the same moment that it "spreads" across the dark sky. So in <reference osisRef="Ps.18.14">Psa 18:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.18.15">15</reference>, the discovering of "the channels of waters" follows the "lightnings." Umbreit translates: "He spreadeth His light upon Himself, and covereth Himself with the roots of the sea" (<reference osisRef="Ps.104.2">Psa 104:2</reference>). God's garment is woven of celestial light and of the watery depths, raised to the sky to form His cloudy canopy. The phrase, "cover Himself with the roots of the sea," is harsh; but the image is grand. <div eID="gen7906" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5289"/><div sID="gen7908" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5289"/>32. Rather, "He covereth (both) His hands with light (lightning, <reference osisRef="Job.37.3">Job 37:3</reference>, Margin), and giveth it a command against his adversary" (literally, the one "assailing" Him, <reference osisRef="Ps.8.2">Psa 8:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.139.20">139:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.21.19">Job 21:19</reference>). Thus, as in <reference osisRef="Job.36.31">Job 36:31</reference>, the twofold effects of His waters are set forth, so here, of His light; in the one hand, destructive lightning against the wicked; in the other, the genial light for good to His friends, &c. (<reference osisRef="Job.36.33">Job 36:33</reference>) [Umbreit]. <div eID="gen7908" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5290"/><div sID="gen7909" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5290"/><hi type="bold">33. noise--</hi>rather, He revealeth it (literally, "announceth concerning it") to His friend (antithesis to adversary, <reference osisRef="Job.36.32">Job 36:32</reference>, so the Hebrew is translated, <reference osisRef="Job.2.11">Job 2:11</reference>); also to cattle and plants (literally, "that which shooteth up"; <reference osisRef="Gen.40.10">Ge 40:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.41.22">41:22</reference>). As the genial effect of "water" in the growth of food, is mentioned, <reference osisRef="Job.36.31">Job 36:31</reference>, so here that of "light" in cherishing cattle and plants [Umbreit]. If English Version, "noise" be retained, translate, "His noise (thunder) announces concerning Him (His coming in the tempest), the cattle (to announce) concerning Him when He is in the act of rising up" (in the storm). Some animals give various intimations that they are sensible of the approach of a storm [Virgil, Georgics, I.373, &c.]. <chapter eID="Job.36"/>
